svg.text: Screws onto an ordinary plastic bottle. Squeezing pushes water through a steel pre-filter, a mycelium bio-filter and a UV-C chamber. No battery, no chip, no charging.
Body: anodised aluminium + food-grade silicone seals, so no plastic in the wet path of the attachment.

g.text: water flow spins a tiny generator
slows flow for a longer UV dose
Swap when squeezing gets hard or the window
stays cloudy (cartridge life still to be tested).
Metal body, meshes and UV unit are reused.
the mycelium breaks down, but the plastic it
caught does not. Return or bin them.

svg.text: D · How to use it, and what each stage really does

g.text: The window has a black/white strip seen through the water.
If the strip looks blurred, the water is cloudy. This needs no power.
Limit: turbidity measures cloudiness, not plastic.
Clear water can still hold microplastics; turbidity sensors are
not microplastic-specific [4]. For a number, a clip-on
Still to prove: mycelium capture at squeeze-flow speed (the lab work
used slow contact), and whether a small turbine gives enough UV-C
dose. If not, fall back to a coin cell. UV-C does not remove or
destroy microplastics; only the filters do.
[1] Wang, H., Dai, S. et al. (2023). Microplastics removal in the aquatic environment via fungal pelletization. Bioresource Technology Reports.
[2] Effectiveness of mycofiltration for removal of contaminants from water: a systematic review protocol (2021). Environmental Evidence.
[3] Innovative microbial water quality management in water distribution systems using in-pipe hydropowered UV disinfection (2024). PubMed ID 39010788.
[4] Govindarajan et al. (2025). Tracking microplastic pathways: real-time IoT monitoring for water quality and public health. MethodsX 15, 103674.
[5] Kulkarni, A. (2025). Economical and novel microplastic detection using an Arduino-based turbidity sensor. Preprint, doi:10.22541/au.176252971.19402178/v1.
